newsitem.title: USA: Nomos unveils new radiation treatment for tumors.
newsitem.headline: Nomos unveils new radiation treatment for tumors.

text.p: Officials at Nomos Corp, a privately held medical technology firm, on Tuesday unveiled a state-of-the-art radiation treatment for brain tumors that they said allows treatment without invasive surgery.
The so-called Peacock laser system also is more advanced than more conventional radiation treatments, including the Gamma knife system used by many hospitals, Nomos officials and doctors said.

The Peacock system is currently used by only 12 U.S. hospitals, but its use will grow rapidly and become routine within the next six to eight years, according to doctors at West Penn Hospital, one of the facilities using the system.
The method delivers doses of radiation that conform precisely to the shape of a tumor so normal surrounding tissue is not damaged.
At a news conference Tuesday, doctors said the treatment is more advanced than the Gamma knife method, which is designed to treat smaller tumors.

"The equipment cost is substantially less and it is able to treat larger tumors in more locations while not endangering other cells," Dr. Robert Selker, director of West Penn's neuro-oncology center, said at a news conference.
The Peacock system is used on benign and malignant tumors that are located in highly sensitive areas, such as on the optic nerve or near the brain stem, making surgery risky.
The method was put into use at West Penn in November 1994 after being cleared by the Food and Drug Administration.
About 500 patients have been treated with the method, 35 of them at West Penn.

West Penn is treating primarily brain tumors with the system, but it is being used at other hospitals to treat esophagus, head, neck, lung, liver and kidney tumors, as well as prostate cancer, said Dr. Mark P. Carol, Nomos president and a former neurosurgeon who developed the technology.
Carol said the Peacock system is less costly for hospitals. The equipment costs about $1.4 million, versus about $4.5 million for Gamma knife equipment.
Both methods cost about the same for a patient, between $10,000 and $20,000, he said.

Dr. Judith Figura, associate chief of West Penn's radiation oncology division, said medical officials decided to publicly unveil the Peacock system as word of the technology spread and media inquiries mounted.
She said the system is unique because of its ability to deliver precision radiation while sparing other areas near a tumor.
Dr. David Waser, professor and acting chairman of Tufts University's radiation oncology department, called the Peacock system "revolutionary."
Tufts has been using the method for three years and has treated about 100 patients.

"It's a concept that I think is radically changing the way we deliver radiation treatment," he said. "We have found it to be very safe...and it appears to decrease toxicity (in a patient's body) compared to coventional radiation therapy."
